own_scenes.place: Baltimore, Oakland, Los Ángeles y Las Vegas
own_scenes.desc: Hijo de Afeni Shakur, pantera absuelta en el juicio de los Panther 21 un mes antes de nacer él, Tupac pasó por la escuela de artes de Baltimore y llegó a la bahía en 1988, donde Leila Steinberg, su mentora, lo metió en Strictly Dope y se lo llevó a Atron Gregory y Shock G: entró en Digital Underground («Same Song»). 2Pacalypse Now (Interscope, 1991), con «Brenda’s Got a Baby» y «Trapped», lo enfrentó a la policía de Oakland, que lo golpeó por cruzar mal, y a Dan Quayle y C. Delores Tucker cuando un abogado culpó a «Soulja’s Story» de la muerte de un policía de Texas. Para Fade Duvernay hubo un Tupac anterior y otro posterior a Bishop, su papel en Juice (1992): la gente empezó a tratarlo como al personaje. Escribía en cinco minutos y cantaba como un instrumento; soñaba con que los raperos volvieran a sus ciudades a organizar a la comunidad («si vendemos un millón de discos, ¿por qué no un millón de votos?»). En noviembre de 1994 lo tirotearon y robaron en los Quad Studios y al día siguiente fue condenado por abuso sexual; desde la cárcel culpó a Bad Boy y a Biggie, y Suge Knight lo fichó para Death Row. «Hit ’Em Up» (1996), el diss más feroz de la historia, avivó la guerra entre costas. El 7 de septiembre de 1996, tras el combate de Tyson en Las Vegas y una pelea con Orlando Anderson, lo tirotearon en el coche de Knight; murió seis días después, con veinticinco años.

notes.text: Abrams creció en las afueras de Los Ángeles a finales de los ochenta, demasiado joven para N.W.A; fue Tupac quien lo convirtió al hip hop: grababa sus canciones de la radio (92.3 The Beat, Power 106) y escondía de su madre la cinta de Me Against the World con su pegatina de Parental Advisory. Su asesinato en 1996 le hizo preguntarse si el género sobreviviría a la pérdida de una de sus estrellas.

refs.q: Instead, for me, the artist who truly stoked those early embers was Tupac Amaru Shakur.
refs.para: Instead, for me, the artist who truly stoked those early embers was Tupac Amaru Shakur. As he did for so many people my age, Pac ignited in me a full devotion to hip-hop music.

refs.q: He was determined to change that.
refs.para: Those first conversations that I had with Pac, we both felt that globally, everybody’s hearts are fucked up. We were all damaged wherever we came from, but the power of money is at the core of most of these issues, and Black people weren’t sitting at any tables. He was determined to change that.

refs.q: Because Tupac, to me, is two very different people. There’s Tupac pre-Bishop, and there’s Tupac post-Bishop.
refs.para: Because Tupac, to me, is two very different people. There’s Tupac pre-Bishop, and there’s Tupac post-Bishop. The Tupac pre-Bishop was very conscious, had a firm understanding on what was taking place politically and socially in the neighborhoods. He was a very insightful, very positive brother.

refs.q: This fucking guy is a musician. His voice was actually an instrument.
refs.para: Deadly Threat (artist, Los Angeles): You know what really tripped me out about Pac? Pac could write a song in maybe ten, fifteen minutes. That’s the ability this dude had. You know what else I learned from hanging around with Pac? This guy is not a fucking rapper. This fucking guy is a musician. His voice was actually an instrument. It’s like he found the beats that actually harmonized with his voice, and with those two combinations, this is how he was killing the game.

refs.q: We sell a million records. Why can’t we get a million votes? We can do it!
refs.para: He’s a very animated dude. Almost seem like he yelling when he talking to you when he gets excited about something. And he would say, “We sell a million records. Why can’t we get a million votes? We can do it!” He said, “You go back to Newark and do what you supposed to do. Treach, go back to East Orange. Ice Cube, go back to L.A. Common, go back to Chicago.”

refs.q: No diss track before or since has carried the same vitriol and consequences as Tupac Shakur’s blistering “Hit ’Em Up,”
refs.para: NO DISS TRACK before or since has carried the same vitriol and consequences as Tupac Shakur’s blistering “Hit ’Em Up,” released in the summer of 1996 as the B-Side to “How Do U Want It.” The track featured the Outlawz, a group Shakur founded upon his prison release, and took direct, confrontational aim at a litany of East Coast rappers. Shakur reserved his most vicious and personal disparagement for the Notorious B.I.G., Puff Daddy (Sean Combs), and Bad Boy Records, whom he held responsible for his being ambushed in New York City.

scenes.name: El hip hop: medio siglo de historia oral
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Un género nacido de la imaginación de chavales abandonados entre las ruinas del Bronx de los setenta que sobrevivió a todo (a una generación mayor que lo rechazaba, a las radios que no lo ponían, a los políticos que lo atacaban) hasta convertirse en la música más popular de Estados Unidos. Abrams hizo más de trescientas entrevistas entre 2018 y 2022 a DJs, artistas, productores, ejecutivos y periodistas para contar su origen y su expansión: del Bronx a los demás distritos «como las venas de un plano del metro», del parque al vinilo, a la Costa Oeste con el gangsta rap y el G-funk, al Sur y más allá. «La lírica es, al fin y al cabo, una forma de tradición oral.»

scenes.name: Digital Underground y KMEL
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Mientras Public Enemy y N.W.A se disputaban la conciencia del hip hop, Shock G (Gregory Jacobs), Chopmaster J y Kenny K formaron en 1987 Digital Underground, un grupo excéntrico devoto de Parliament-Funkadelic que absorbió a Raw Fusion (Money-B, DJ Fuze). KMEL, la emisora pop de Keith Naftaly, cambió el Top 40 por hip hop, R&B, reggae y house, rompió a Hammer, Vanilla Ice o DJ Quik e inventó el Summer Jam. Tras «Underwater Rimes», Tommy Boy publicó Sex Packets (1990): «The Humpty Dance» de su alter ego Humpty Hump los hizo estrellas pop, con «Doowutchyalike» y «Freaks of the Industry». Precursores del G-funk de Dr. Dre y trampolín de Tupac. Shock G murió en 2021.

scenes.name: Gangsta rap: el relevo del lite metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El rap, sobre todo el gangsta, conquista al público adolescente blanco masculino que antes estaba con el lite metal: ritmos pegadizos en lugar de melodía y flow en lugar de virtuosismo con la guitarra, con la autenticidad de sus orígenes pandilleros subrayada por los asesinatos de figuras como Tupac Shakur. El Senado repite contra él las audiencias que una década antes se hicieron contra el metal, ahora presididas por Carol Moseley Braun y con C. Delores Tucker en el papel de Tipper Gore, y acusándolo de misoginia y violencia contra las mujeres; como pasó con el PMRC, la cruzada solo aumenta sus ventas.

podcast.title: Coachella Hologram Performance (2012)
podcast.body: In 2012, a virtual Tupac Shakur made a striking appearance at Coachella during a set by Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg. Though marketed as a hologram, it was technically an advanced projection using Pepper's Ghost techniques, appearing "awfully lifelike" and marking a pivotal moment in the development of simulated live performances. "Then in 2012, a very dead two-pock Shakur showed up at Coachella during a set featuring Dr. Dre and Snoop Dog."

podcast.title: Early Career with Digital Underground
podcast.body: Before launching his successful solo career, Tupac Shakur gained experience in the music industry as a roadie, dancer, and backup singer for the group Digital Underground. This formative period helped him get his start in performing. "Tupac Shakur was a roadie, dancer and backup singer for Digital Underground and that got him started on his journey to a solo career."

podcast.title: Videos for Branding
podcast.body: Tupac utilized his music videos not merely to sell a single or album, but as a strategic tool for branding. In the hip-hop world, videos became essential for conveying themes of money, status, luxury, and identity, thereby solidifying an artist's public image. "Tupac, Missy Elliott, and Dr. Dre used their videos as branding, not just to sell a single or a album."
